---
title: "Why AI Chat Math Won't Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard"
date: 2026-10-30
categories: [tools, latex, word, texbridge]
---

Copy a formula out of ChatGPT and paste it into Word and you get one of three
disappointments: a picture you cannot edit, a line of raw `\frac{a}{b}`, or a
row of mangled symbols. None of them is a Word equation.

That is not Word being obtuse. The formula on screen was never an equation,
and the thing Word wants is a format no chat site produces. This post is about
what sits on each side of that gap, and what has to go on the clipboard to
bridge it.

## A formula on a web page is not a formula

Nothing in a web page is an equation. A chat site renders math with a
JavaScript library, almost always MathJax or KaTeX, and what lands in the DOM
is one of:

- **SVG.** MathJax's SVG output draws each glyph as vector paths. Visually
  perfect, semantically nothing. Copy it and you have copied a drawing.
- **Styled HTML.** MathJax's CommonHTML output and KaTeX build the formula
  from spans with careful CSS. What looks like a fraction bar is a `<span>`
  with a border.
- **An image.** A few sites still render server-side to PNG.

The visual layer is a dead end in all three cases. What rescues the situation
is that the libraries also leave the semantics in the page, out of sight.
KaTeX emits a hidden MathML copy next to the visual one; MathJax ships an
Assistive MathML extension that, in its own words, "inserts hidden MathML for
the usual output renderers." And MathML has a slot for the original source:

``` html
<annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{RT}{V_m - b}</annotation>
```

So the LaTeX you typed is usually still on the page, one layer down. Finding
it reliably is harder than it sounds: the attribute names, the element
structure and even whether the hidden copy exists at all vary by renderer, by
renderer version, and by how a given site configures it. But the principle
holds everywhere. Anything that moves chat math somewhere useful works from
that hidden semantic layer, not from the pixels on top.

## What Word stores

Word's native equation format is **OMML**, Office Math Markup Language. An
equation inside a `.docx` is a tree of `m:` elements in `word/document.xml`,
in the namespace

```
http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math
```

Nothing on a web page produces OMML. That is the problem in one sentence.

## Route 1: linear format, typed by hand

Word accepts an equation written on one line and then "built up" into two
dimensions. It supports two linear formats, and the difference matters:
**UnicodeMath**, Microsoft's own compact notation, and **LaTeX**.

`Alt` + `=` opens an equation field; type or paste the linear source; `Ctrl` +
`=` builds it up. `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `=` goes back.

Two limits before you rely on it. Microsoft describes LaTeX input as new to
Microsoft 365 subscribers, so on a perpetual licence do not assume it is
there. And Word's LaTeX is a dialect: `\begin{}` and `\end{}` are
unsupported, so environments do not work and you write `\matrix{a & b \\ c &
d}` instead, while `\eqarray`, `\Middle`, `\ldiv` and `\dsmash` are not
supported at all.

This route works, it needs no tooling, and it does not scale past a few
formulas.

## Route 2: hand Word its own format on the clipboard

This is the route that actually scales, and the one people are surprised
exists.

When you paste into Word, Word does not read the plain-text flavour of the
clipboard. It reads the **`text/html`** flavour — and it reads it as *Word's
own HTML*, a dialect that has carried Office-specific markup since the days of
"Save as Web Page". Word understands OMML embedded there, and it understands
markup addressed to itself that every other application is required to skip.

That second property is what makes the whole thing work. A single clipboard
payload can carry a real OMML equation for Word and readable LaTeX for
everything else, and each reader takes its own branch. Paste into Word and you
get a native equation; paste the same clipboard into a plain text editor and
you get `$\frac{RT}{V_m - b}$`.

The practical consequence is that a tool doing this well is not "converting
LaTeX to Word". It is walking the page's MathML into OMML, wrapping that in a
Word-flavoured HTML payload, and writing `text/html` and `text/plain` together
so the paste degrades sensibly wherever it lands. Getting the conversion right
across real-world formulas — matrices, cases, multi-line alignments,
over- and under-braces — is where the actual work is.

## Route 3: write the file

Skip the clipboard and generate the `.docx` yourself. A Word file is a zip of
XML; the math goes in under the `officeDocument/2006/math` namespace and the
document body under `wordprocessingml/2006/main`. Most work, most control, and
the only route that handles a whole chat transcript at once rather than one
formula at a time.

## Why Word on the web is different

Word in a browser cannot accept a pasted equation from any application,
because a browser tab never receives the rich clipboard payload the desktop
app does. The conditional-comment trick needs Word itself reading the
clipboard, and in the web app there is no Word reading the clipboard.

The workaround is Route 1, explicitly: `Insert` → `Equation`, paste the linear
source into the box at the top of the panel, press `Space`, insert. It works,
and it is also where the dialect limits bite hardest, because matrices, cases
and multi-line equations are exactly what that box cannot build.

## PowerPoint, Excel, Google

One line in Microsoft's documentation explains a great deal of confusion:

> All other Office applications support only UnicodeMath.

PowerPoint, Excel and Outlook do not take LaTeX input. A workflow built on
pasting LaTeX into Word does not transfer to a slide deck, which is why
getting a formula into PowerPoint means OMML or an image.

Google Docs and Slides have no equation format worth targeting at all. There a
high-resolution image is not a compromise, it is the correct answer.

## Picking a route

| Route | Result | Where it works | Main cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Linear, typed | Native, editable | Word desktop; LaTeX needs 365 | Manual; dialect gaps |
| OMML in HTML clipboard | Native, editable | Word, PowerPoint desktop | Must generate OMML |
| Generated `.docx` | Native, editable | Anywhere Word opens | Most work |
| Image | Not editable | Everywhere, incl. Google | Fixed resolution |

There is no single format that is both easy to produce and universally
accepted, which is the whole reason this is annoying.

## The tool

I write thermodynamics, and a post like
[Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State](../potentials-for-eos/)
carries over two hundred equations. Rebuilding those by hand in Word for a
report was not something I was willing to keep doing, so I built
[TeXbridge](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dhncopmbldpljhclmnaadlgomflnadlm),
a Chrome and Edge extension that does the above: reads the hidden semantic
layer, converts to OMML, and picks a target format based on where the formula
is going. If a site renders something it handles badly, there is a
[support page and FAQ](https://khanhbvu.github.io/texbridge/).

The mechanism is worth knowing either way. If you understand that the LaTeX is
hiding in an annotation element, and that Word reads `text/html` with a
conditional comment in it, you can get a formula where it needs to go by hand.
